A Trip Through Space:
From Earth to the Multiverse

Let's go on a trip! We start at home and zoom out, step by step, until we reach the biggest idea in science.

Before we fly: our space cameras

We take pictures of space with telescopes. Hubble flies 540 km above Earth. James Webb sits 1.5 million km away, with a mirror covered in real gold!

1 Earth

Here we are, on our blue planet. It feels huge, but it is just a tiny dot in space.

Zoom out!

2 Solar System

Earth goes around the Sun with 7 other planets. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us.

Zoom out!

3 Milky Way, our galaxy

Our Sun is one of billions of stars in a giant spinning swirl called the Milky Way.

Find us! The small circle on the right is where our Solar System lives. (Picture: Scale of Space)

Inside our galaxy, telescopes see amazing things:

A star nursery. This glowing pink cloud of gas and dust is where new stars are being born. (Picture: NASA, Webb telescope)

Space towers. Giant pillars of gas and dust, taller than many solar systems put together.

The Cat's Eye Nebula. A dying star puffing off its outer layers, like blowing bubbles. It is 4,400 light-years away. (Picture: Hubble and Euclid telescopes)

Zoom out!

4 Our galaxy's neighbours

The Milky Way has more than 50 neighbour galaxies, like Andromeda. Together with many more, we belong to a giant family of about 100,000 galaxies called Laniakea.

Did you know? Light from Andromeda takes 2.5 million years to reach us. On a dark night, far from city lights, you can see it as a faint, fuzzy smudge without a telescope!
Zoom out!

5 The cosmic web

Now galaxies look like tiny dots. They line up along glowing threads, like a spider web.

Wow! Every bright dot is a whole galaxy. Can you find our Milky Way in the circle? (Picture: Scale of Space)

Zoom out!

6 Everything we can see

This is the observable universe: everything whose light has had time to reach us. Artists have drawn it as one big circle with us in the middle.

How to read these drawings: the Sun and planets are in the middle. Then come stars, then galaxies, then the cosmic web. The glowing rim is the oldest light of all. (Pictures: artists' illustrations of the observable universe)

The farther out we look, the older the light, because it has been travelling for so long.

Zoom out!

7 The universe's baby picture

At the very edge of what we can see is a faint glow from when the universe was a baby, only 380,000 years old.

Three baby pictures, each sharper than the last. The newest, from the Planck satellite (bottom), shows tiny speckles. Those speckles were the seeds that grew into every galaxy! (Picture: Big Think)

Zoom out!

8 The multiverse? (a big idea)

What is beyond everything we can see? Nobody knows yet.

Imagine this: the small circle is our whole visible universe. Some scientists think there could be more universes out there, like bubbles in a bath. This is called the multiverse. (Picture: Scale of Space)

Remember: the multiverse is only an idea. Nobody has ever seen another universe, and scientists are still asking if we can ever check. (Picture: Scale of Space)

Amazing space facts

QuestionAnswer
How old is the universe?About 13.8 billion years
How many galaxies can we see?About 2 trillion
How old was the universe in its baby picture?About 380,000 years
Does the universe have a middle?No!
Is the multiverse real?Nobody knows yet
Try this tonight: look up! Every star you see is in our own Milky Way.
